segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jude, a slave of Jesus Christ and brother of James, to those who are called, loved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, while I was making every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I found it necessary to write and urge you to contend for the faith handed down once for all to the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For certain people have slipped in unnoticed—people who long ago were written down for this condemnation, ungodly, who turn the grace of our God into debauchery and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I want to remind you, though you have come to know everything once for all, that Jesus, after saving a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the angels who did not keep their own domain but left their proper dwelling he has kept in everlasting chains beneath the gloom for the judgment of the great day;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them, which in the same way as these gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after flesh of another kind, are set out as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet in the same way these people also, in their dreaming, defile the flesh, reject authority, and slander the glorious ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Michael the archangel, when he was disputing with the devil and arguing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him, but said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “The Lord rebuke you!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But these people slander whatever they do not understand, and whatever they do know by instinct, like unreasoning animals, by these things they are destroyed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Woe to them! For they have gone the way of Cain, have rushed headlong into Balaam’s error for pay, and have perished in Korah’s rebellion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the hidden reefs at your love feasts, feasting with you without fear, shepherding themselves; waterless clouds carried along by winds; late-autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, the Lord is coming with his holy myriads,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: to carry out judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all the works of ungodliness they have committed in their ungodliness, and of all the harsh things ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own desires; their mouths speak bombast, and they flatter people for the sake of advantage.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: how they used to tell you,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly desires.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the ones who cause divisions, merely natural people, who do not have the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And have mercy on some, who are wavering;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: save others, snatching them out of the fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling and to set you before his glory without blemish and with great joy,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the only God our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, power, and authority, before every age, and now, and for all the ages. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servant” or “bond-servant”. In the Septuagint “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David, and both the ownership and the honor are probably heard here.

notes.traditional: kept for Jesus Christ; preserved in Jesus Christ
notes.note: The Greek dative can mean “kept for Jesus Christ” (guarded until his coming) or “kept by Jesus Christ”. Most modern translations and commentators prefer “for”, as here. The verb “keep” runs through the letter (verses 6, 13, 21).

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s holy people”.

Manuscripts differ here: many read “the Lord”, a few read “God”, and several of the earliest and most important read “Jesus”, which the SBLGNT and other recent critical editions adopt. On that reading Jude credits the pre-existent Jesus with the rescue from Egypt. The placing of “once for all” in the sentence also varies among manuscripts.

notes.phrase: the angels who did not keep their own domain
notes.traditional: the angels which kept not their first estate
notes.note: Jude alludes to the Jewish tradition, built on Genesis 6:1–4 and developed at length in 1 Enoch, of angels who abandoned heaven to take human wives and were bound in darkness until the judgment. The word rendered “domain” can also mean “position of authority” or “rule”. The play on “keep” is deliberate: they did not keep their place, so God has kept them in chains.

notes.phrase: went after flesh of another kind
notes.traditional: going after strange flesh; pursued unnatural desire
notes.note: The Greek is literally “went after other flesh”. Since “in the same way as these” most naturally points back to the angels of verse 6, many scholars take the phrase to refer to the men of Sodom seeking intercourse with angels (Genesis 19), which is the mirror image of angels seeking human women. Others take it more generally of sexual perversion, as renderings such as “unnatural desire” do.

notes.traditional: blaspheme the glorious ones; speak evil of dignities
notes.note: In first-century Greek this verb meant abusive or defamatory speech against anyone, while modern English “blaspheme” is reserved for speech against God. The “glorious ones” (literally “glories”) are almost certainly angelic beings, so “slander” is used; several modern versions keep “blaspheme” here. The same verb recurs in verse 10, and the related noun is rendered “slanderous” in verse 9.

notes.phrase: arguing about the body of Moses
notes.note: This story is not in the Old Testament. Early Christian writers say Jude took it from a Jewish work known as the Assumption (or Testament) of Moses, the relevant part of which has not survived. Michael’s words echo Zechariah 3:2. The phrase rendered “a slanderous judgment” may instead mean “a condemnation for slander”, in which case Michael declined to pass sentence on the devil’s slander himself.

The Greek word normally means a rock or reef in the sea on which ships are wrecked, and that is the sense adopted here. Some translations render “blemishes” or “stains”, taking it as equivalent to a similar word used in the parallel at 2 Peter 2:13 and echoed in “stained” in verse 23. Both senses are defended by scholars.

The plural of the word “love” is used here for the shared meals of the early Christian communities, at which the Lord’s Supper was probably celebrated. This is the earliest clear use of the term in that sense.

notes.phrase: the Lord is coming with his holy myriads
notes.traditional: the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints
notes.note: Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, a Jewish work widely read in the period though not part of the Hebrew Scriptures. The “holy myriads” are the countless angels of God’s retinue, not human believers. The Greek verb is in the past tense (“came”), a prophetic idiom that presents the future event as already seen.

The adjective describes people who live by ordinary human life alone, as opposed to people animated by God’s Spirit; Paul uses it the same way in 1 Corinthians 2:14. “Sensual” (KJV) now suggests bodily indulgence, which is not the point. Modern versions vary among “worldly”, “natural” and “following mere natural instincts”.

notes.phrase: have mercy on some, who are wavering
notes.traditional: of some have compassion, making a difference
notes.note: The text of verses 22–23 is among the most uncertain in the New Testament: manuscripts give two groups or three, and some read “convince” or “refute” in place of the first “have mercy”. The three-group form translated here follows the SBLGNT and most modern editions. The word rendered “wavering” could also mean “disputing”, as it does in verse 9.

notes.phrase: before every age, and now, and for all the ages
notes.traditional: before all time and now and forever
notes.note: The Greek uses the word “age” twice, spanning past, present and future: literally “before the whole age, and now, and into all the ages”. Most translations render “before all time, now and forever”, which is the meaning. “Age” is kept in both places so that the repetition remains visible.

candidates.reason: Recurs in every part of the New Testament, and translators split between “slave”, “servant” and “bond-servant”, especially in self-designations like this one.
The common address in the letters is rendered “beloved”, “dear friends” or “loved ones”, and the choice affects visible links with ἀγάπη and ἀγαπάω.
Occurs in 1 Corinthians 2:14, 15:44–46, James 3:15 and here, and is rendered variously as “natural”, “unspiritual”, “worldly” and “sensual”; the contrast with πνευματικός needs one decision.
The word group (ἀσεβής, ἀσέβεια, ἀσεβέω) recurs in Romans, the Pastorals, the Petrine letters and Jude, with translators varying among “ungodly”, “impious” and “godless”.
Appears in vice lists across the Gospels and letters with widely varying English (licentiousness, sensuality, debauchery, lewdness), and should be uniform.
